narrative:
The model predicted a 97% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction to assess an applicant's likelihood of successfully completing law school and passing the bar, your application was rejected.

The three factors that most strongly influenced this decision, in order of importance, were your class rank in the third year of law school, your LSAT score, and your first-year class rank. All three pushed the prediction strongly toward failure rather than success.

Your third-year ranking placed you in the bottom decile of your class, far below the average of accepted students who typically ranked near the middle. This was the single biggest reason the model doubted your chances. Your LSAT score of 25 was also well below the average of 37 seen among accepted applicants, adding further weight toward a negative outcome. Finally, your first-year ranking in the lowest decile, compared to an average around the sixth decile for successful applicants, reinforced the same concern about consistent academic performance.

Although your undergraduate GPA of 3.60 exceeds the accepted average and your middle-income background and full-time status are fairly typical, these positive or neutral factors were not enough to offset the three dominant signals.

To improve your prospects, focus on raising your academic performance and consider retaking the LSAT to demonstrate stronger analytical skills. Strengthening these two areas would likely change how future models evaluate your application. (248 words)
